input:
In this worked example, we will estimate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor that raises natural gas from an inlet pressure of 1 bar to a discharge pressure of 6 bar, which corresponds to an overall pressure ratio of 6. The inlet temperature of the gas is 313 K, and the compression is to be treated as isentropic, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the value 1.4 being held constant by the calculation throughout the compression. Under these conditions, the discharge temperature obtained from the isentropic relation is 522 K.

This represents a temperature rise of some 209 K above the inlet temperature, which is a considerable increase and illustrates the substantial heating effect that accompanies the compression of a gas even in a single stage. The treatment is deliberately simple, and its simplicity is precisely what makes the result useful as a reference point against which the behaviour of the actual machine can be judged. It is interesting to note that the discharge temperature is governed by just three quantities in this treatment, namely the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio, so that a change in any one of them will alter the result accordingly.

It is important to emphasise, however, that the isentropic estimate deliberately excludes mechanical losses, and for this reason the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine will be higher than the 522 K calculated here. The figure of 522 K should therefore be regarded as an idealised, best-case value rather than as a realistic prediction of the temperature that will actually be observed in practice, and any decisions based upon it should be taken with this important qualification clearly in mind at all times.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 6 bar, a pressure ratio of 6, and the discharge temperature is to be estimated for isentropic compression. The inlet temperature is 313 K and the heat-capacity ratio is 1.4. For isentropic compression, the discharge temperature is fixed by the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio; substitution of the stated values gives a discharge temperature of 522 K.

The rise over the inlet temperature is 209 K. Isentropic compression is the reversible adiabatic path: no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, and no mechanical loss appears inside the calculation, so the whole of the temperature rise is the rise the pressure ratio itself produces. The estimate also inherits a simplification from its inputs: a single heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 is held across the whole compression, and the result is conditional on that holding.

The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than 522 K. The difference between the measured value and the isentropic figure is the part of the rise the model does not contain: mechanical losses in a real machine appear as additional internal energy in the gas, and the discharge temperature records them. The isentropic estimate is therefore a floor for the discharge temperature at this pressure ratio, not a prediction of it, and it is to be used as a floor: a cooling duty or a material limit set on 522 K alone would be set on the lowest discharge temperature the compression can produce, with the real machine operating above it by the amount its losses add. Used in that way, the estimate disciplines the design discussion: any allowance made above it is an allowance for losses, made explicitly, rather than a correction applied silently to a figure that was never a prediction.
